_meta.purpose: Herb monographs for the professional-herbalist consultation engine.
_meta.how_to_read: risk = how careful to be by default (low: kitchen or gentle herbs; moderate: needs a screen of medicines and conditions; high: only offered when no medicines are taken). preg/bf values: ok | limited (allowed with the stated limit) | avoid. min_age is the youngest age for therapeutic use; smaller food amounts are fine earlier. interactions use the medicine class ids from herbalist_rules.json; severity major = do not combine, moderate = combine only with a note and prescriber awareness, minor = mention only.
_meta.accuracy_note: Amounts are typical published or monograph ranges for healthy adults. EMA/HMPC figures for peppermint leaf and valerian root, the Cochrane/AAFP honey-for-cough evidence, the licorice blood-pressure/pregnancy cautions and the pregnancy herb review were checked against the source documents; the rest reflect widely published herbal references (ESCOP, WHO monographs, German Commission E, NCCIH, LiverTox) and traditional systems, and should be reviewed by a qualified herbalist or pharmacist before use with real patients.

ginger.name: Ginger (adrak, sonth, zanjabeel)
ginger.tradition: Ayurveda, Unani and TCM: a warming digestive, anti-nausea and circulation herb; the base of most cold and cough kadhas.
ginger.evidence_note: Good evidence for nausea (motion, post-operative, pregnancy); moderate for period pain; limited for joint pain.

prep.how: Simmer 3-4 thin slices (about 2 g fresh root) in 1 cup of water for 10 minutes; add honey or lemon if you like.
prep.duration: a few days for symptoms, up to 1-2 weeks

prep.how: Stir 1/4 to 1/2 teaspoon (0.5-1 g) into warm water, tea or food.
prep.freq: up to 3 times a day (keep the total from all sources under about 4 g a day)

cautions: Large amounts can cause heartburn, mouth irritation or loose stools.
Concentrated ginger supplements have a mild blood-thinning effect; stop them 1-2 weeks before surgery.
ginger.preg_note: Ginger is widely used for pregnancy nausea. Keep to about 1 g of dried ginger (or 3-4 thin fresh slices) a day in divided amounts, and tell your midwife or doctor.
ginger.child_note: Small amounts in food are fine from age 2.

interactions.note: Ginger in food or tea amounts is usually fine, but concentrated ginger can add to the blood-thinning effect. Keep to tea and food amounts and tell your prescriber.
May lower blood sugar slightly; keep monitoring as usual.
May add a small blood-pressure-lowering effect.

sources: NCCIH Herbs at a Glance: Ginger
WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, vol 1
Narrative review on ginger in nausea and vomiting of pregnancy (J Res Med Health)

peppermint.name: Peppermint (pudina)
peppermint.tradition: Used across Europe, the Middle East and South Asia for gas, cramps, nausea and tension headache.
peppermint.evidence_note: Enteric-coated peppermint oil has good trial support for irritable-bowel cramping; the leaf tea has long traditional use for dyspepsia and gas (EMA/HMPC monograph, long-standing use).

prep.how: 1.5-3 g dried leaf (about 1 heaped teaspoon) in 100-150 ml of boiling water, covered, steeped 10 minutes (EMA/HMPC).
prep.freq: up to 3 times a day, after meals
prep.duration: up to 2 weeks; see a doctor if symptoms last longer

prep.how: Use a capsule labelled enteric-coated, about 0.2 ml (180-225 mg) of oil, swallowed whole with water 30 minutes before meals.
prep.duration: up to 8 weeks for irritable-bowel cramping

prep.form: diluted peppermint oil on the temples
prep.how: Mix 1 drop of peppermint essential oil into about 1/2 teaspoon of carrier oil (roughly 10 percent) and dab a little on each temple and the forehead, away from the eyes.

cautions: Can worsen heartburn and reflux by relaxing the valve at the top of the stomach.
Never put menthol or peppermint oil on the face or chest of babies and young children.
Do not swallow undiluted essential oil.
peppermint.preg_note: No harm has been shown from an occasional cup of weak peppermint tea, but safety is not established; avoid concentrated oil and large amounts, especially in early pregnancy.
peppermint.bf_note: Large amounts may reduce milk supply; an occasional cup is fine.
peppermint.child_note: EMA does not recommend peppermint tea under 4 years.

interactions.note: Concentrated peppermint oil can slightly raise levels of some medicines (for example some statins and calcium-channel blockers); tea is much less likely to.
Acid reducers can make enteric-coated oil capsules dissolve too early, causing heartburn.

sources: EMA/HMPC European Union herbal monograph on Mentha x piperita leaf (2020), checked
NCCIH Herbs at a Glance: Peppermint Oil

chamomile.name: Chamomile (babuna, gul-e-babunah)
chamomile.tradition: One of the most used gentle herbs in Europe and Unani medicine: calming, soothing to the gut and skin.
chamomile.evidence_note: Traditional use for mild stomach upset and sleep; small trials for anxiety and sleep; creams and compresses for mild skin irritation.

prep.how: 1-2 heaped teaspoons (2-4 g) dried flowers in a cup of just-boiled water, covered, steeped 10 minutes.
prep.freq: up to 3-4 times a day; one cup 30-60 minutes before bed for sleep
prep.duration: as needed, ideally up to 2 weeks at a time

prep.how: Steep 2 teaspoons of flowers in a cup of hot water for 10-15 minutes, cool completely, then soak a clean cloth and press on the skin for 10 minutes. The same cooled tea can be used as a mouth rinse.

cautions: People allergic to ragweed, daisies or marigolds can react to chamomile.
Can add a little to the effect of sedatives.
chamomile.preg_note: Reviews have raised concern about regular chamomile tea in pregnancy, especially the last trimester. If used at all, make it an occasional weak cup and check with your midwife.
chamomile.child_note: Weak, cooled tea only for young children.

interactions.note: Contains coumarin-type compounds; a few case reports with warfarin. Moderate tea use is generally fine; tell your prescriber.
May add mild drowsiness.

sources: EMA/HMPC monograph on Matricaria flower
NCCIH Herbs at a Glance: Chamomile
Review: herbal teas in pregnancy (PMC7384490), checked

fennel.name: Fennel seed (saunf)
fennel.tradition: Chewed after meals across South Asia for gas and bloating; a classic carminative in Europe and Unani medicine.
fennel.evidence_note: Traditional carminative with small trials for bloating, colic cramps and period pain.

prep.how: Lightly crush 1/2 to 1 teaspoon (1-2 g) seeds, cover with a cup of boiling water, steep 10-15 minutes and strain.
prep.freq: up to 3 times a day, after meals

prep.how: Chew 1/2 teaspoon of plain roasted saunf slowly after meals.

cautions: Do not use fennel essential oil internally.
Regular medicinal amounts have estrogen-like activity.
fennel.preg_note: Cooking amounts are fine, but regular fennel tea is best avoided in pregnancy because of its estrogen-like activity.
fennel.bf_note: Occasional tea is common, but heavy daily use has been linked to rare problems; keep it modest.
fennel.child_note: Not recommended as a medicinal tea under 4 years.

interactions.note: Estrogen-like activity; avoid regular medicinal use with hormonal medicines or tamoxifen.
May reduce absorption of ciprofloxacin; take at least 2 hours apart.

sources: EMA/HMPC monograph on Foeniculum vulgare fruit
Review: herbal teas in pregnancy (PMC7384490), checked

ajwain.name: Carom seeds (ajwain)
ajwain.tradition: A first-line kitchen remedy in South Asia for gas, indigestion and colicky pain; used in steam and warm poultices for congestion.
ajwain.evidence_note: Strong traditional use; the active oil (thymol) has lab evidence, but there is little clinical trial data.

prep.how: Chew 1/2 teaspoon (about 1 g) ajwain with a pinch of black salt and follow with a few sips of warm water, or simmer 1/2 teaspoon in a cup of water for 5 minutes and sip.
Add 1 tablespoon ajwain to a bowl of hot water and breathe the steam gently from arm's length for 5 minutes.
prep.duration: a few days for a blocked nose

cautions: Strongly heating; can aggravate acidity or ulcers.
ajwain.preg_note: Cooking amounts are fine, but medicinal amounts are traditionally avoided in pregnancy.
ajwain.child_note: A tiny pinch in food for younger children is traditional.
sources: Traditional use (Ayurveda, Unani)
Pharmacological review of Trachyspermum ammi

cumin.name: Cumin (zeera, jeera)
cumin.tradition: Jeera water is a household digestive; part of the classic CCF (cumin-coriander-fennel) tea in Ayurveda.
cumin.evidence_note: Small studies in dyspepsia and irritable-bowel symptoms; mainly traditional.

prep.how: Simmer 1/2 to 1 teaspoon cumin seeds in 1 cup water for 5-10 minutes, strain and sip warm.
Simmer 1/2 teaspoon each of cumin, coriander and fennel seeds in 3 cups of water for 10 minutes, strain and sip through the day.

cautions: Heating; large amounts may cause heartburn.
cumin.preg_note: Cooking amounts are fine; avoid concentrated medicinal amounts.
cumin.child_note: Food amounts only for small children.

interactions.note: May lower blood sugar slightly.

sources: Traditional use (Ayurveda, Unani)
Small trials in irritable-bowel symptoms

cardamom.name: Green cardamom (elaichi)
cardamom.tradition: A cooling, aromatic digestive and breath freshener in South Asian cooking.
cardamom.evidence_note: Mostly traditional; small studies on blood pressure and nausea.

prep.how: Lightly crush 2-3 pods and steep in a cup of hot water or tea for 5-10 minutes.

cautions: May provoke colic in people with gallstones.
sources: Traditional use (Ayurveda, Unani)

hing.name: Asafoetida (hing)
hing.tradition: A pinch in lentils and beans in South Asian cooking, used for gas; in warm water or as a paste on the belly.

prep.how: Dissolve a small pinch (about 1/8 teaspoon) of hing in half a cup of warm water and sip, or cook it in a little ghee or oil at the start of a dal or vegetable dish.

cautions: Never give hing preparations to infants.
hing.preg_note: Cooking pinches are fine; avoid medicinal amounts.
hing.child_note: Cooking amounts only under 12; infants should not have hing.

interactions.note: Has mild blood-thinning properties.
May add a small blood-pressure-lowering effect.

sources: Traditional use (Ayurveda, Unani)

lemon_balm.name: Lemon balm (Melissa, bilsan)
lemon_balm.tradition: A calming, lemon-scented herb for nervous tension, restless sleep and nervous stomach; the cream is used on cold sores.
lemon_balm.evidence_note: Small trials for mild anxiety and sleep; topical cream shortens cold-sore healing in trials.

prep.how: 1-2 teaspoons (1.5-4.5 g) dried leaf in a cup of just-boiled water, covered, steeped 10 minutes.
prep.freq: 1-3 times a day; one cup in the evening for sleep
prep.duration: up to 4 weeks, then take a break

prep.form: lemon balm cream (1 percent leaf extract)
prep.how: Use a pharmacy cream labelled for cold sores and apply to the tingling area at the first sign.

cautions: May cause drowsiness; avoid driving if it makes you sleepy.
lemon_balm.preg_note: Safety is not established; best avoided.

interactions.note: Adds to drowsiness from sedating medicines.
May interfere with thyroid hormone activity; avoid regular use with thyroid medicine unless your prescriber agrees.

sources: EMA/HMPC monograph on Melissa officinalis leaf
NCCIH-listed trials on lemon balm

passionflower.name: Passionflower
passionflower.tradition: A European and American calming herb for nervous restlessness and light sleep.
passionflower.evidence_note: Small trials suggest benefit for mild anxiety and sleep quality.

prep.how: About 1 teaspoon (1-2 g) dried herb in a cup of just-boiled water, covered, steeped 10 minutes.
prep.freq: 1-3 times a day; one cup 30-60 minutes before bed for sleep

cautions: Can cause drowsiness and dizziness; avoid driving afterward.
Do not combine with alcohol.
passionflower.preg_note: Animal data suggest it can stimulate the uterus.

interactions.note: Adds to drowsiness from sedating medicines.
Contains harmala-type compounds; do not combine with MAO inhibitors.
May have a mild effect on clotting.

sources: EMA/HMPC monograph on Passiflora herb
NCCIH Herbs at a Glance: Passionflower

valerian.name: Valerian root
valerian.tradition: The classic European sleep and nervous-tension root.
valerian.evidence_note: EMA: well-established use for mild nervous tension and sleep disorders; the effect builds over 2-4 weeks and trial results are mixed.

prep.how: Tea: 0.3-3 g (about 1/2 to 1 teaspoon) cut root in 150 ml boiling water, covered, steeped 10-15 minutes. Or a standardised extract per the label (EMA reference 450-600 mg dry extract).
prep.freq: once, 30-60 minutes before bed (may also be used up to 3 times a day for nervous tension)
prep.duration: 2-4 weeks; see a doctor if no better after 2 weeks

cautions: May impair driving and machinery use.
Vivid dreams, headache or morning grogginess in some people.
Not for acute use: the effect builds over days to weeks.
Avoid alcohol with it.

interactions.note: Adds to the effect of sedating medicines; EMA advises this combination only with medical supervision.
Possible minor effect on liver enzymes.

stop_if: dark urine, yellow skin or eyes, or upper-right abdominal pain
sources: EMA/HMPC EU herbal monograph on Valeriana officinalis root (draft, 2015), checked
LiverTox: valerian

lavender.name: Lavender
lavender.tradition: A calming aromatic used for stress, sleep and minor skin complaints.
lavender.evidence_note: Inhaled lavender oil and a standardised oral extract (silexan) have trial support for anxiety and sleep; EMA lists traditional use for mild stress and sleep.

prep.how: Put 2-3 drops of lavender essential oil on a tissue or cotton pad and place it near your pillow, or use a diffuser for 20-30 minutes before bed.
1 teaspoon (about 1 g) culinary dried flowers in a cup of just-boiled water, covered, steeped 10 minutes.

cautions: Do not swallow lavender essential oil (use tea or a labelled capsule).
Repeated skin use of lavender or tea tree oil has been linked to breast tissue growth in prepubertal boys.
lavender.preg_note: Aromatherapy and an occasional cup of tea are generally considered fine; avoid oral oil.
lavender.child_note: Light aromatherapy only for young children.

interactions.note: May add to the effect of sedating medicines.

stop_if: headache or nausea from the scent
sources: EMA/HMPC monograph on Lavandula angustifolia flower
NCCIH Herbs at a Glance: Lavender

ashwagandha.name: Ashwagandha (Indian ginseng)
ashwagandha.tradition: The best-known Ayurvedic adaptogen for stress, low stamina and sleep.
ashwagandha.evidence_note: Several small to medium trials show lower stress and better sleep over 6-12 weeks; rare cases of liver injury have been reported.

prep.how: Standardised root extract 300 mg once or twice a day with food, or 1-3 g root powder stirred into warm milk at night, from a reputable tested brand.
prep.duration: 4-8 weeks, then take a break; up to 3 months at most without review

cautions: Rare reports of liver injury: stop if you notice dark urine, yellow skin or eyes, itching or severe tiredness.
Can raise thyroid hormone levels.
May cause sleepiness or stomach upset.

interactions.note: Can raise thyroid hormones and add to thyroid medicine.
May stimulate the immune system and work against immune-suppressing medicines.
Adds to drowsiness from sedating medicines.
May lower blood sugar further.
May lower blood pressure further.

stop_if: dark urine, yellow skin or eyes, itching or abdominal pain
sources: NCCIH Herbs at a Glance: Ashwagandha
LiverTox: ashwagandha
Randomised trials on ashwagandha and stress

tulsi.name: Holy basil (tulsi)
tulsi.tradition: Sacred in Ayurveda; leaves are taken daily in tea and kadha for colds, cough, stress and general resilience.
tulsi.evidence_note: Strong traditional use; small trials for stress and blood sugar; no strong evidence for colds.

prep.how: 5-8 fresh leaves, or 1 teaspoon dried leaf, in a cup of just-boiled water, covered, steeped 5-10 minutes; honey and ginger can be added.
prep.duration: as needed, up to a few weeks

cautions: Animal studies suggest an anti-fertility effect, so avoid regular use if you are trying to conceive.
May lower blood sugar slightly.
tulsi.preg_note: Culinary leaf amounts are fine; avoid concentrated or regular large amounts.
tulsi.child_note: A few leaves in a weak tea are traditional for children.

interactions.note: May have a mild effect on clotting.
May lower blood sugar slightly.

sources: Traditional use (Ayurveda)
Systematic review: Ocimum sanctum clinical trials (2017)

turmeric.name: Turmeric (haldi)
turmeric.tradition: Haldi doodh (turmeric milk) is the household remedy for colds, aches and wounds across South Asia.
turmeric.evidence_note: Food amounts are very safe. Standardised curcumin extracts show moderate evidence for osteoarthritis pain; supplements carry more risk than the spice.

prep.how: Warm 1 cup of milk (or plant milk), stir in 1/2 to 1 teaspoon (1.5-3 g) turmeric powder and a pinch of black pepper, simmer 3-5 minutes and sweeten with honey if you like.
prep.duration: a few days for a cold; ongoing in cooking

prep.how: Mix 1/2 teaspoon turmeric with enough honey or aloe gel to make a paste, apply to a minor skin spot for 15 minutes and rinse (it stains).

cautions: Concentrated curcumin supplements (especially with piperine) have been linked to rare liver injury; prefer the spice.
Can aggravate gallstones and kidney-stone formers (oxalate).
Binds iron, which matters if you are low in iron.
turmeric.preg_note: Food amounts are fine; avoid supplements.
turmeric.child_note: Food amounts only for small children.

interactions.note: Concentrated curcumin may add to the blood-thinning effect; food amounts are rarely a problem.
May lower blood sugar further.
Curcumin, especially with piperine, can raise levels of some medicines.
May raise levels of tacrolimus and similar medicines.
May interact with some chemotherapy and antiviral medicines.

stop_if: dark urine or yellow skin or eyes
sources: NCCIH Herbs at a Glance: Turmeric
LiverTox: turmeric
EFSA and Italian Ministry of Health statements on turmeric supplements and liver injury

black_pepper.name: Black pepper (kali mirch)
black_pepper.tradition: Part of every kadha: warming, stimulating mucus clearance and appetite.
black_pepper.evidence_note: Traditional use; piperine increases absorption of many substances.

prep.how: Add 2-3 crushed peppercorns or a pinch of powder (1/8 to 1/4 teaspoon) to a cup of tea or kadha, or take with honey.

cautions: Piperine can raise blood levels of some medicines.

interactions.note: Piperine can raise levels of some medicines; keep to a pinch.
Piperine can raise levels of phenytoin and carbamazepine; keep to a cooking pinch.

sources: Traditional use (Ayurveda, Unani)
Pharmacokinetic reviews of piperine

cinnamon.name: Cinnamon (dalchini)
cinnamon.tradition: Warming digestive and cold remedy; used in kadha and spiced teas.
cinnamon.evidence_note: Mixed small trials on blood sugar; traditional for digestion and colds.

prep.how: Simmer a 5 cm stick (or 1/2 teaspoon powder) in a cup of water for 10 minutes. Prefer Ceylon cinnamon; cassia should stay under about 1/2 teaspoon (1 g) a day because of coumarin.
prep.duration: as needed, up to a few weeks

cautions: Cassia cinnamon contains coumarin, which can stress the liver at higher intakes.

interactions.note: May lower blood sugar further.
Cassia contains coumarin.

sources: EFSA opinion on coumarin in cinnamon
NCCIH Cinnamon

clove.name: Clove (laung)
clove.tradition: A whole clove held against a sore tooth is a classic remedy; also in kadha for cough.
clove.evidence_note: Eugenol is a recognised dental analgesic; the whole spice is a long-standing cough and toothache remedy.

prep.how: Add 1-2 whole cloves to a cup of tea or kadha and steep 5-10 minutes.
Hold one whole clove against the sore tooth and gently bite, or put 1 drop of clove oil in 1/2 teaspoon of carrier oil on a cotton bud and dab on the tooth. Never apply undiluted oil to gums.
prep.duration: until you can see a dentist

cautions: Undiluted clove oil burns gums and tissue.
Concentrated eugenol is toxic to the liver in large amounts; never swallow the oil.
clove.preg_note: Cooking amounts only; avoid the oil.
clove.child_note: Do not use clove oil for children.

interactions.note: Eugenol can add to the blood-thinning effect.
May lower blood sugar slightly.

sources: Traditional use (Ayurveda, Unani)
ESCOP and WHO notes on clove oil

thyme.name: Thyme
thyme.tradition: A classic European expectorant and cough herb.
thyme.evidence_note: Thyme-containing cough syrups show benefit for chesty cough in trials; EMA lists traditional use for cough with mucus.

prep.how: 1/2 to 1 teaspoon (1-2 g) dried thyme in 150 ml of just-boiled water, covered, steeped 10 minutes; add honey for adults and children over 1.

cautions: Use culinary thyme, not the essential oil, by mouth.
thyme.preg_note: Cooking amounts only; avoid medicinal teas.
thyme.child_note: Weak tea with honey for ages 4 and over (honey only over 1 year).
sources: EMA/HMPC monograph on Thymus vulgaris herb
ESCOP monograph on thyme

sage.name: Sage
sage.tradition: A gargle for sore throat and mouth; tea for night sweats and hot flushes.
sage.evidence_note: Sage lozenges and spray show benefit for sore throat; small studies for hot flushes.

prep.how: Pour 100 ml of boiling water over 2.5 g (about 1 teaspoon) dried sage leaf, steep 10 minutes, strain, cool to warm and gargle (do not swallow).
1 teaspoon dried leaf in a cup of just-boiled water, steeped 10 minutes.

cautions: Contains thujone: do not exceed the stated amounts or duration.
sage.preg_note: Avoid; thujone may harm the pregnancy.

interactions.note: May lower blood sugar slightly.
May add mild sedation.
Thujone may lower the seizure threshold.

sources: EMA/HMPC monograph on Salvia officinalis leaf
WHO monograph on sage leaf

licorice.name: Licorice root (mulethi, mulaithi)
licorice.tradition: Mulethi is chewed or brewed for sore throat and dry cough in South Asian homes; a soothing demulcent in Unani and TCM.
licorice.evidence_note: Soothing for sore throat and cough; whole licorice raises blood pressure and lowers potassium at high intakes.

prep.how: Simmer 1/2 teaspoon (about 1-2 g) dried root in a cup of water for 10 minutes and sip warm.

cautions: Glycyrrhizin in real licorice causes salt and water retention and lowers potassium: raises blood pressure and can trigger rhythm problems.
Do not use for more than about 2 weeks; avoid licorice sweets in large amounts.
licorice.preg_note: May increase preterm birth risk; avoid.

interactions.note: Licorice raises blood pressure and works against blood-pressure medicines.
Adds to potassium loss from water pills.
Low potassium makes digoxin toxicity more likely.
Can increase steroid side effects.
May reduce the effect of warfarin and other blood thinners; best avoided.
Has estrogen-like effects.

stop_if: headache, swelling, palpitations or muscle weakness
sources: Merck Manual Professional: Licorice, checked
EFSA and WHO notes on glycyrrhizin intake

dgl.name: DGL (deglycyrrhizinated licorice)
dgl.tradition: A modern form of licorice with the blood-pressure-raising compound removed, used for heartburn and stomach lining comfort.
dgl.evidence_note: Small trials in dyspepsia; mostly traditional and clinical-practice use.

prep.how: Chew 400-800 mg (per the label) 20 minutes before meals; make sure the label says deglycyrrhizinated.
prep.freq: up to 3 times a day before meals

cautions: Only use products clearly labelled deglycyrrhizinated.
dgl.preg_note: Not enough data; ask your doctor or midwife.
sources: Clinical herbal practice references
Small trials of DGL in dyspepsia

marshmallow_root.name: Marshmallow root (khatmi)
marshmallow_root.tradition: A mucilage-rich root that coats irritated throat and gut.
marshmallow_root.evidence_note: EMA lists traditional use for dry cough and irritated mouth and throat.

prep.how: Soak 2-5 g (1-2 teaspoons) cut root in a cup of cold water for 2-8 hours, strain and sip; or use lozenges per the label.

cautions: Take other medicines about an hour away; the mucilage can slow absorption.
marshmallow_root.preg_note: Not enough data; occasional use is generally considered low risk but ask your doctor.

interactions.note: May lower blood sugar slightly.

sources: EMA/HMPC monograph on Althaea officinalis root

slippery_elm.name: Slippery elm
slippery_elm.tradition: A soothing demulcent for irritated throat and stomach, taken as a gruel or lozenge.

prep.how: Stir 1 teaspoon (2-4 g) powder into a cup of warm water or oatmeal to a thin paste, or use lozenges per the label.

cautions: Take other medicines 1-2 hours apart.
sources: Clinical herbal practice references

honey.name: Honey (shahd)
honey.tradition: Universal household remedy for cough and sore throat; also a topical wound dressing (medical grade).
honey.evidence_note: A Cochrane review of three trials (568 children) found honey reduces cough frequency better than no treatment or placebo and about as well as dextromethorphan (summarised by AAFP).

prep.how: Take straight from the spoon or stirred into warm water or herbal tea, before bed. Ages 1-5: 1/2 teaspoon; ages 6-11: 1 teaspoon; ages 12 and over: 2 teaspoons.
prep.freq: at bedtime, and up to 2-3 times a day if the cough is bad

prep.form: medical-grade honey on a minor wound
prep.how: On a clean minor cut or scrape, apply a thin layer of sterile medical-grade honey (for example manuka dressings sold at pharmacies), cover with a dressing and change it daily. Do not use raw kitchen honey on deep wounds.
prep.freq: once a day, at dressing change

cautions: Never give honey to a child under 12 months (infant botulism).
Honey is sugar: count it if you have diabetes.
sources: AAFP: Honey for acute cough in children (summary of Cochrane review)
WHO guidance on demulcents for cough

elder.name: Elderflower and elderberry
elder.tradition: Elderflower tea is a European diaphoretic for the start of a cold; cooked elderberry syrup for flu.
elder.evidence_note: Small trials suggest elderberry extract can shorten flu symptoms by a day or two.

prep.how: 1-2 teaspoons (3-5 g) dried elderflower in a cup of hot water, covered, steeped 10-15 minutes; drink hot. Elderberry syrup: use a commercial cooked product per its label.
prep.duration: 3-5 days at the start of a cold

cautions: Raw elderberries, leaves and stems are toxic (cyanogenic compounds): only cooked or commercial products.

interactions.note: May stimulate the immune system and work against immune-suppressing medicines.
May add a mild diuretic effect.

sources: EMA/HMPC monograph on Sambucus nigra flower
NCCIH Herbs at a Glance: Elderberry

echinacea.name: Echinacea
echinacea.tradition: The North American immune herb, taken at the first sign of a cold.
echinacea.evidence_note: Reviews are inconclusive; some preparations may modestly reduce the length or chance of a cold.

prep.how: A standardised product (tincture, tablet or tea) used exactly as the label directs, starting at the first sign of a cold.

cautions: Not for long-term use.
echinacea.preg_note: Short-term use has not shown harm but data are limited; ask your doctor.

interactions.note: Stimulates the immune system and works against immune-suppressing medicines.
Possible minor effect on liver enzymes.

sources: NCCIH Herbs at a Glance: Echinacea
Cochrane review on echinacea for colds

garlic.name: Garlic (lehsun)
garlic.tradition: A kitchen medicine for colds, cough and circulation across many traditions.
garlic.evidence_note: Modest effects on cholesterol and blood pressure in trials; may reduce frequency of colds in one trial.

prep.how: Crush 1 clove (about 3-4 g), leave 10 minutes so the active compound forms, and swallow with honey or food, or stir into soup at the end of cooking.

cautions: Raw garlic can irritate the stomach; never put raw garlic on skin (it burns).

interactions.note: Garlic supplements can add to the blood-thinning effect; food amounts are generally fine.
Garlic supplements can lower levels of some HIV medicines (for example saquinavir).
May lower blood sugar slightly.
May add a small blood-pressure-lowering effect.

sources: NCCIH Herbs at a Glance: Garlic
Cochrane review on garlic for colds

aloe_vera.name: Aloe vera gel (ghritkumari)
aloe_vera.tradition: Cooling gel for burns, sun-irritated and itchy skin.
aloe_vera.evidence_note: Limited evidence for first-degree burns and sunburn; traditional soothing use.

prep.how: After cooling the burn under cool running water for 10-20 minutes, spread a thin layer of pure gel (scooped from the inner leaf, or a product that is at least 95 percent aloe with no alcohol or fragrance).

cautions: Do not put on deep, infected or heavily bleeding wounds.
Do not swallow the yellow latex or whole-leaf products (strong laxative).
sources: NCCIH Herbs at a Glance: Aloe Vera
Systematic review: aloe vera for burns

calendula.name: Calendula (marigold)
calendula.tradition: A gentle skin-healing flower for minor cuts, rashes and dry skin.
calendula.evidence_note: Trials support calendula ointment for wound healing and radiation dermatitis; traditional for dry and irritated skin.

prep.how: Use a cream or ointment with calendula flower extract (about 2-5 percent) in a thin layer on clean, unbroken or lightly broken skin.

cautions: Not for deep or infected wounds.
calendula.preg_note: Topical use is generally considered low risk; avoid taking it by mouth.
sources: EMA/HMPC monograph on Calendula flower
Cochrane review on calendula for radiation dermatitis

tea_tree.name: Tea tree oil
tea_tree.tradition: Australian antiseptic oil for acne, dandruff and fungal skin infections.
tea_tree.evidence_note: Trials support 5 percent gel for mild to moderate acne and 5 percent shampoo for dandruff; 10-50 percent solutions are used for athlete's foot.

prep.form: tea tree 5 percent gel or shampoo
prep.how: Use a commercial product with about 5 percent tea tree oil: dab the gel on spots, or lather the shampoo into the scalp for 3 minutes before rinsing.
prep.freq: gel 1-2 times a day; shampoo daily to 3 times a week

prep.form: diluted tea tree for fungal skin
prep.how: Use a cream or solution containing 10-25 percent tea tree oil, or mix 5 drops into 1 teaspoon of carrier oil to start; apply to clean, dry skin and let it dry.

cautions: Never swallow; keep away from eyes.
Always patch test: allergic skin reactions are common.
Toxic to cats and dogs.
Repeated use on prepubertal boys has been linked to breast tissue growth.
tea_tree.preg_note: Diluted use on small skin areas is considered low risk; avoid large areas.
sources: NCCIH Tea Tree Oil
Randomised trials: tea tree for acne and dandruff
Cochrane-style reviews on topical antifungals

witch_hazel.name: Witch hazel (distilled)
witch_hazel.tradition: An astringent for insect bites, minor irritation and haemorrhoid discomfort.
witch_hazel.evidence_note: EMA lists traditional use for minor skin inflammation and small wounds.

prep.how: Dab on a bite or irritated skin with a cotton pad.
prep.amount: a few drops on a pad

cautions: Choose alcohol-free distilled witch hazel; keep away from eyes.
sources: EMA/HMPC monograph on Hamamelis virginiana

plantain_leaf.name: Plantain leaf (barg-e-bartang)
plantain_leaf.tradition: A folk poultice for stings, bites and small scrapes. Not the banana-like fruit.
plantain_leaf.evidence_note: Traditional use; some lab evidence for soothing and healing.

prep.how: Pick a clean leaf from an unsprayed spot away from the roadside, wash it, crush or chew it into a wet pulp and press on the bite or sting for 10-15 minutes.

cautions: Only use plants you can identify with certainty.
sources: Traditional use
EMA/HMPC monograph on Plantago lanceolata leaf

neem.name: Neem (nim)
neem.tradition: Neem leaf water and paste are traditional for scalp, acne and itchy skin.
neem.evidence_note: Lab antibacterial and antifungal activity; small studies for acne, dandruff and scalp; used topically only here.

prep.how: Simmer a handful of fresh neem leaves in 1 litre of water for 10-15 minutes, cool, strain and use as a final rinse for the scalp or skin.

prep.form: diluted neem oil on skin spots
prep.how: Dilute neem oil 1 part to 10 parts carrier oil and dab on a patch-tested spot.

cautions: Never swallow neem oil (toxic, especially to children).
Patch test first.
neem.preg_note: Neem has anti-fertility and pregnancy-ending effects in animals; avoid.
sources: WHO and Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia references
Small clinical studies on neem for scalp and acne

amla.name: Amla (Indian gooseberry)
amla.tradition: A vitamin C-rich fruit central to Ayurvedic rejuvenative tonics and hair oils.
amla.evidence_note: Rich in vitamin C and tannins; small trials on cholesterol and blood sugar; hair benefits are traditional.

prep.how: One fresh fruit a day, or 1/2 to 1 teaspoon (2-3 g) powder stirred into water or honey.
Warm amla-infused oil, or mix amla powder with water or yoghurt to a paste, massage into the scalp, leave 30 minutes and wash.

cautions: Tannin-rich; may cause stomach upset on an empty stomach.

interactions.note: May have a mild effect on clotting.
May lower blood sugar slightly.

sources: Traditional use (Ayurveda)
Small clinical trials of Phyllanthus emblica

triphala.name: Triphala
triphala.sci: Terminalia chebula, T. bellirica, Phyllanthus emblica
triphala.tradition: The classic Ayurvedic three-fruit bowel tonic, taken at night.
triphala.evidence_note: Small trials suggest mild laxative and digestive effects; quality of commercial products varies (contamination reports).

prep.how: Stir 1/2 to 1 teaspoon (2-3 g) into a cup of warm water and drink at bedtime, from a tested brand.

cautions: Stop if it causes loose stools or cramps.
Use tested, reputable products.

interactions.note: May have a mild effect on clotting.
May lower blood sugar slightly.

sources: Traditional use (Ayurveda)
Systematic review of Triphala clinical studies

psyllium.name: Psyllium husk (isabgol)
psyllium.tradition: The household bulk fibre across South Asia, often stirred into water or curd.
psyllium.evidence_note: Well-established for constipation, and for modestly lowering cholesterol.

prep.how: Stir 1 heaped teaspoon (about 5 g) into a full glass (250 ml) of water, drink at once, then drink another glass of water. Begin with once a day and increase slowly.

cautions: Always take with plenty of water; dry husk can cause choking or blockage.
Take other medicines at least 2 hours apart.
psyllium.child_note: Half the dose for ages 6-11, with plenty of fluid.

interactions.note: Can reduce thyroid medicine absorption; take it at least 4 hours apart.
May reduce lithium absorption; separate doses.
May lower blood sugar slightly.
May reduce carbamazepine absorption; separate doses.

stop_if: difficulty swallowing, chest or throat tightness
sources: NCCIH and clinical guidelines for psyllium
Cochrane and meta-analyses on fibre for constipation

flaxseed.name: Flaxseed (alsi)
flaxseed.tradition: Ground seeds as a gentle bulking laxative and omega-3 food.
flaxseed.evidence_note: Moderate evidence for mild constipation and cholesterol.

prep.how: Stir 1-2 tablespoons (10-20 g) freshly ground seed into yoghurt, oats or a smoothie and drink a full glass of water.

cautions: Whole seeds mostly pass through undigested; grind them.
Drink plenty of fluid.

interactions.note: Omega-3 content may have a mild effect on clotting.
May lower blood sugar slightly.

sources: NCCIH Flaxseed and Flaxseed Oil
Systematic reviews on flaxseed and constipation

senna.name: Senna (sana makki)
senna.tradition: A strong stimulant laxative used short term for occasional constipation.
senna.evidence_note: Well-established for short-term relief of occasional constipation (EMA/HMPC).

prep.how: Use an over-the-counter senna product exactly per the label (commonly 7.5-15 mg sennosides at night).

cautions: Do not use for more than a week: it can cause dependence and potassium loss.
Not for weight loss.
senna.preg_note: Only short-term, with your doctor's agreement.

interactions.note: Both lower potassium.
Low potassium makes digoxin toxicity more likely.
Both lower potassium.

stop_if: severe cramps, vomiting or watery diarrhoea
sources: EMA/HMPC monograph on Senna leaf
German Commission E

hibiscus.name: Hibiscus tea (karkade)
hibiscus.tradition: A tart red tea used for blood pressure and cooling in Egypt, the Middle East and South Asia.
hibiscus.evidence_note: Several small trials show modest reductions in blood pressure.

prep.how: 1-2 teaspoons (1.5-2 g) dried calyces in a cup of just-boiled water, steeped 5-10 minutes.
prep.duration: ongoing for several weeks, with blood pressure checks

cautions: Can lower blood pressure further: monitor if you take blood-pressure medicine.

interactions.note: May add to the blood-pressure-lowering effect; check your blood pressure and tell your prescriber.
May change levels of hydrochlorothiazide.
May lower blood sugar.

sources: Meta-analyses of Hibiscus sabdariffa on blood pressure
NCCIH Hibiscus

fenugreek.name: Fenugreek (methi)
fenugreek.tradition: Soaked methi seeds are a household remedy for blood sugar, digestion and hair.
fenugreek.evidence_note: Small trials show modest improvements in blood sugar; traditional for digestion and hair.

prep.how: Soak 1 teaspoon (about 5 g) seeds in a cup of water overnight; drink the water and chew the softened seeds in the morning.
Soak 2 tablespoons seeds overnight, grind to a paste, massage into the scalp, leave 30 minutes and wash.

cautions: May cause gas or loose stools; can make sweat and urine smell of maple syrup.
fenugreek.preg_note: May stimulate the uterus; avoid medicinal amounts.

interactions.note: Can lower blood sugar further; monitor closely.
May add to the effect of warfarin.

sources: NCCIH Herbs at a Glance: Fenugreek
Meta-analyses on fenugreek and blood glucose

karela.name: Bitter melon (karela)
karela.tradition: A bitter vegetable and juice used traditionally for blood sugar.
karela.evidence_note: Small trials with modest, inconsistent effects on blood sugar.

prep.how: Eat one small cooked bitter melon as part of a meal a few times a week; if using juice, keep to about 30-50 ml diluted with water.

cautions: Can cause low blood sugar and stomach upset; seeds and concentrated juice are the riskiest parts.
karela.preg_note: May cause bleeding or contractions; avoid.

interactions.note: Can cause low blood sugar with diabetes medicines; keep portions small and monitor.

sources: Traditional use
Systematic reviews on Momordica charantia and glycaemic control

kalonji.name: Black seed (kalonji)
kalonji.tradition: Revered in Unani and Islamic tradition; seeds and oil taken daily as a general tonic.
kalonji.evidence_note: Small trials show benefit for allergic rhinitis symptoms and modest effects on blood sugar and blood pressure.

prep.how: 1/2 to 1 teaspoon (1-2 g) seeds sprinkled on food, or crushed into a spoonful of honey, or 1/2 teaspoon of seed oil.

cautions: Large amounts may upset the stomach.
kalonji.preg_note: Medicinal amounts may stimulate the uterus; cooking amounts only.

interactions.note: May lower blood sugar further.
May lower blood pressure further.
May have a mild effect on clotting.

sources: Traditional use (Unani)
Systematic reviews of Nigella sativa clinical trials

rosemary.name: Rosemary (hasalban)
rosemary.tradition: A scalp-stimulating oil for hair, and a culinary herb.
rosemary.evidence_note: One randomised trial found rosemary oil as effective as 2 percent minoxidil for androgenetic alopecia after 6 months; evidence is still preliminary.

prep.how: Mix 3-4 drops of rosemary essential oil into 1 tablespoon (15 ml) of carrier oil (such as coconut, jojoba or olive oil). Patch test first. Massage into the scalp for 5 minutes, leave 30-60 minutes (or overnight) and wash out.

cautions: Never use undiluted oil on skin; keep away from eyes.
Do not swallow rosemary essential oil.
rosemary.preg_note: Medicinal and essential-oil use is best avoided; culinary amounts are fine.

interactions.note: Large oral amounts may have a mild effect on clotting; topical use is unlikely to matter.

sources: Panahi et al. 2015, randomised trial of rosemary oil vs minoxidil
EMA/HMPC monograph on Rosmarinus officinalis leaf

green_tea.name: Green tea
green_tea.tradition: A daily antioxidant-rich tea; the extract is used in topical skin products.
green_tea.evidence_note: Moderate evidence for mild alertness and as a topical for acne; concentrated extracts are the safety concern, not the tea.

prep.how: 1 teaspoon (2 g) leaf in a cup of hot (not boiling) water, steeped 3 minutes.
prep.freq: 1-3 cups a day, not near bedtime

prep.form: cooled green tea as a skin toner
prep.how: Steep a tea bag in hot water, cool completely, and dab on clean skin with a cotton pad.

cautions: Avoid concentrated green tea extracts and capsules: rare liver injury.
Contains caffeine; reduces iron absorption if drunk with meals.
green_tea.preg_note: Count the caffeine; keep total caffeine under about 200 mg a day (around 3 cups of green tea).

interactions.note: Vitamin K in tea can reduce the effect of warfarin; keep intake steady.
Reduces iron absorption; drink tea 2 hours away from iron tablets.
Large amounts may change levels of some medicines.

sources: NCCIH Herbs at a Glance: Green Tea
LiverTox: green tea extract

cranberry.name: Cranberry
cranberry.tradition: A North American fruit used to reduce repeated urinary infections.
cranberry.evidence_note: Reduces repeat UTIs in women with recurrent infection (prevention, not a treatment for an active infection).

prep.how: 240 ml (1 cup) of unsweetened cranberry juice daily, or a capsule delivering about 36 mg proanthocyanidins per label.

cautions: Does not treat an active urinary infection: that needs testing and usually antibiotics.

interactions.note: Case reports with warfarin; keep intake steady and tell your prescriber.

sources: Cochrane review: cranberries for preventing UTIs (2023)
NCCIH Cranberry

willow_bark.name: White willow bark
willow_bark.tradition: The original source of salicin (aspirin's cousin) for aches, back pain and fever.
willow_bark.evidence_note: Standardised extracts reduce low-back and osteoarthritis pain in trials; it works like a mild aspirin and shares its risks.

prep.how: A standardised extract providing 120-240 mg salicin a day, per the label.
prep.duration: short courses of up to 4 weeks

cautions: Acts like aspirin: can cause stomach bleeding and affect clotting.
Not for under-18s because of the Reye syndrome risk with salicylates.

interactions.note: Adds to the bleeding risk.
Duplicates the NSAID effect and raises stomach and kidney risk.
Can raise methotrexate toxicity.
Salicylates can reduce the effect of water pills and strain the kidneys.

stop_if: stomach pain, black stools or ringing in the ears
sources: ESCOP monograph on Salix cortex
NCCIH Willow Bark

feverfew.name: Feverfew
feverfew.tradition: A European herb for migraine prevention.
feverfew.evidence_note: Some trials show fewer migraines with regular use; results are mixed.

prep.how: A standardised product (commonly 100-150 mg dried leaf or extract daily) per the label.
prep.duration: give it 4-6 weeks; this is for prevention, not for an attack

cautions: Chewing fresh leaves can cause mouth ulcers.
Stopping abruptly can cause rebound headaches.

interactions.note: May increase bleeding risk.

sources: NCCIH Herbs at a Glance: Feverfew
Cochrane review on feverfew for migraine prevention

arnica.name: Arnica gel
arnica.tradition: A topical for bruises, sprains and muscle soreness.
arnica.evidence_note: An arnica gel performed similarly to ibuprofen gel in a small trial for hand osteoarthritis; evidence for bruising is mixed.

prep.how: Apply a thin layer of a commercial arnica gel to unbroken skin over the bruise or sore muscle and rub in gently.

cautions: Never on broken skin and never swallow herbal arnica (toxic).
arnica.preg_note: Topical use on unbroken skin is generally considered low risk but ask first.
sources: NCCIH Arnica
Randomised trial: arnica gel vs ibuprofen gel in hand osteoarthritis

capsaicin.name: Capsaicin cream (chilli)
capsaicin.tradition: A counter-irritant for joint and muscle pain and nerve pain.
capsaicin.evidence_note: Moderate evidence for osteoarthritis and neuropathic pain with regular use.

prep.how: Apply a thin layer of an over-the-counter cream (0.025-0.075 percent) to the sore joint or muscle and wash your hands well afterward.
prep.duration: give it 2-4 weeks; the early burning fades

cautions: Not on broken skin, near eyes, or under a tight bandage or heat pad.
sources: Cochrane review: topical capsaicin for chronic pain
NCCIH Capsaicin

boswellia.name: Boswellia (shallaki, frankincense)
boswellia.tradition: An Ayurvedic gum resin for joint stiffness and inflammation.
boswellia.evidence_note: Several small trials show reduced knee osteoarthritis pain after 4-12 weeks.

prep.how: A standardised extract (commonly 300-500 mg, 30-65 percent boswellic acids) with food, per the label.

cautions: May cause stomach upset.

interactions.note: Possible minor effect on liver enzymes.

sources: NCCIH Boswellia
Systematic review: Boswellia serrata in osteoarthritis

vitex.name: Chaste tree (vitex, agnus castus)
vitex.tradition: A European herb for premenstrual symptoms and breast tenderness.
vitex.evidence_note: Trials support benefit for premenstrual symptoms over at least three cycles.

prep.how: A standardised dried-fruit extract (commonly 20-40 mg a day) taken in the morning, per the label.

cautions: Can cause nausea, headache or acne at first.

interactions.note: May interfere with contraceptives and hormone therapy.

sources: EMA/HMPC monograph on Agnus castus fruit
NCCIH-listed trials on vitex for PMS

black_cohosh.name: Black cohosh
black_cohosh.tradition: A North American herb for menopausal hot flushes.
black_cohosh.evidence_note: Trial results for hot flushes are mixed; rare liver injury reports.

prep.how: A standardised extract per the label (often 20-40 mg twice a day).

cautions: Stop and see a doctor if you develop dark urine, yellow skin or eyes, or upper-right abdominal pain.

interactions.note: Effects with hormone therapy are unclear; discuss with your prescriber.
Possible minor effect.

stop_if: dark urine, yellow skin or eyes, or abdominal pain
sources: NCCIH Herbs at a Glance: Black Cohosh
LiverTox: black cohosh

saffron.name: Saffron (zafran, kesar)
saffron.tradition: A mood-lifting spice in Persian, Unani and Ayurvedic medicine.
saffron.evidence_note: Several randomised trials found saffron extract helpful for mild to moderate depressive symptoms over 6-8 weeks; it should sit alongside medical review, not replace it.

prep.form: saffron in milk or a standardised extract
prep.how: A pinch (about 0.1-0.3 g, 8-10 threads) steeped in warm milk, or a standardised extract of about 30 mg a day (15 mg twice daily) per the label.
prep.duration: 6-8 weeks, with a review if mood has not lifted

cautions: More than about 1.5 g a day is unsafe; more than 5 g is toxic.
Can trigger mania in people with bipolar disorder.
saffron.preg_note: Medicinal amounts may stimulate the uterus; culinary pinches are fine.

interactions.note: Do not add to antidepressants without your prescriber's agreement.
May lower blood pressure slightly.
May have a mild effect on clotting.

stop_if: agitation, racing thoughts or reduced need for sleep
sources: Meta-analyses of saffron for depression
NCCIH-listed trials

oatmeal.name: Colloidal oatmeal
oatmeal.tradition: Oat baths and creams for itchy, dry or eczema-prone skin.
oatmeal.evidence_note: Colloidal oat products are recognised skin protectants with good evidence for itch and dryness.

prep.how: Stir 1 cup finely ground plain oats (or a colloidal oatmeal product) into a lukewarm bath, soak 10-15 minutes, pat dry and moisturise within 3 minutes; or use a colloidal oat cream.

cautions: The tub can be slippery.
sources: US FDA skin protectant monograph for colloidal oatmeal
Reviews of colloidal oatmeal in atopic dermatitis

coconut_oil.name: Virgin coconut oil
coconut_oil.tradition: A daily skin and hair oil across South Asia.
coconut_oil.evidence_note: Small trials show benefit for dry and atopic skin; may clog pores in acne-prone skin.

prep.how: Warm a teaspoon between your palms and spread over damp skin straight after bathing; on hair, massage into the scalp and lengths before washing.

cautions: Can worsen acne on the face.
sources: Randomised trials of coconut oil in atopic dermatitis

eucalyptus.name: Eucalyptus
eucalyptus.tradition: Steam inhalation for blocked nose and chest congestion.
eucalyptus.evidence_note: The active compound (cineole) helps symptoms of acute bronchitis and sinusitis in trials of capsule forms; steam use is traditional.

prep.how: Add 1-2 drops of eucalyptus oil to a bowl of hot (not boiling) water, lean over at arm's length with eyes closed and breathe gently for 5-10 minutes. Stop if it irritates.

cautions: Never swallow eucalyptus oil.
Do not use near the face of children under 6; the bowl of hot water is a scald risk.
eucalyptus.preg_note: Gentle steam is generally considered low risk; avoid the oil on skin.
eucalyptus.child_note: Not near the face of young children.

interactions.note: Eucalyptol may slightly affect liver enzymes; unlikely with inhaled use.

sources: EMA/HMPC monograph on Eucalyptus globulus leaf and oil
ESCOP monograph on eucalyptus oil

st_johns_wort.name: St John's wort
st_johns_wort.tradition: A European herb for mild to moderate low mood.
st_johns_wort.evidence_note: Trials support benefit for mild to moderate depression, but it interacts with a very large number of medicines.

prep.how: Only a standardised product, exactly per the label, and only after a pharmacist has checked all your medicines.
prep.duration: 4-6 weeks then review with a clinician

cautions: Makes the skin more sun-sensitive.
Strongly changes how many medicines work, including contraceptives.

interactions.note: Risk of serotonin syndrome.
Do not combine.
Can cause contraceptive failure.
Reduces the effect of warfarin and some other blood thinners.
Can cause transplant rejection by lowering medicine levels.
Lowers levels of many HIV and cancer medicines.
Lowers levels of many medicines.
Lowers digoxin levels.
Lowers anti-seizure medicine levels.
Can add to or change sedative effects.

sources: NCCIH Herbs at a Glance: St. John's Wort
EMA/HMPC monograph on Hypericum perforatum
